title: Charlie's Mom Has Cancer

jokes.text: Charlie deflects his mom trying to have a conversation: 'We don't talk, and it's good that way.'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Kelly says she offered to do laundry so they could talk, implying warmth and closeness.
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately rejects the premise — their not talking is by design and preferable.
jokes.explanation: Classic Charlie selfishness delivered with total sincerity. The character integration is strong — this is exactly the kind of emotional avoidance Charlie exhibits throughout the series. Good economy; it lands fast.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: We don't talk, and it's good that way.

jokes.text: Mac arrives with everyone's laundry and thanks Mrs. Kelly, then Charlie brushes off her attempt to talk: 'Ooh, talky, talky, talky, talky, talky.'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Kelly tries again to bring something important up after the boys dismiss her.
jokes.punchline: Charlie mocks her attempt to speak with a dismissive sing-song 'talky talky talky' and says they have a big day — which turns out to be drinking at a bar.
jokes.explanation: The 'talky talky' childish dismissal is a solid character beat — Charlie treating his sick mother like an inconvenience. The reveal that the 'big day' is just drinking at the bar amplifies the selfishness joke nicely.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Ooh, talky, talky, talky, talky, talky.

jokes.text: Charlie cuts his mom off mid-sentence with 'Ooh, talky, talky, talky, talky, talky' and pivots to their plans to drink beers.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Kelly tries to bring up something important while Charlie and Mac rush to leave.
jokes.punchline: Charlie mocks her desire to talk with a baby-talk dismissal and reveals their 'big day' is just going to drink beers.
jokes.explanation: 'Talky talky talky' is a brilliantly childish way for Charlie to dismiss his mother, perfectly characterizing his arrested development. The reveal that their big plans amount to 'polish off a couple beers' adds a second layer. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie's Mom
dialogue.line: Um, I have cancer.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, but I got to... I'm sorry. What?

jokes.text: 'But how? You don't even smoke.' — Mac's reaction to learning Mrs. Kelly has lung cancer.
jokes.setup: Mrs. Kelly has just revealed she has lung cancer.
jokes.punchline: Mac's first instinct is to fact-check whether she earned the cancer, not to express sympathy.
jokes.explanation: Very economical. The joke is entirely in Mac's misplaced priorities — his first response to a cancer diagnosis is essentially 'that doesn't add up' rather than compassion. Short, sharp, and character-revealing.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: But how? You don't even smoke.

jokes.text: Frank insists his mind is sharp: 'The point is my mind is as sharp as a... what do you call it?' then can't remember the word for 'knife.'
jokes.setup: Frank is defending his mental sharpness against accusations of being scammed.
jokes.punchline: He loses the word 'knife' mid-sentence while claiming his mind is razor-sharp.
jokes.explanation: Near-perfect structural irony. The joke is self-contained and self-undermining — the proof of his declining mind IS the punchline delivered in real-time. The form IS the content. Frank can't finish his own claim to sharpness because he's not sharp. High structure score because the joke couldn't be better built.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: How many pairs of shoes have you lost this month, Frank?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Three.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Hmm?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Four.

jokes.text: 'Thumbtack.' — Frank randomly blurting the word during an unrelated conversation about the cancer scam.
jokes.setup: Earlier Frank couldn't finish 'sharp as a...' The conversation has since moved on entirely to the cancer scam.
jokes.punchline: Frank suddenly and irrelevantly announces 'Thumbtack' — the word he was searching for minutes ago — as if continuing a train of thought nobody else is on.
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best jokes. The callback is structurally perfect: the audience has forgotten the original beat, so the non-sequitur 'Thumbtack' lands as pure absurdity before recognition clicks in — a double-layered laugh. The economy is exceptional (one word). And it deepens the joke about Frank's mental deterioration: it took him several minutes to retrieve that word. High marks across the board; genuinely well-crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: The point is my mind is as sharp as a... what do you call it? Um, it's a... Knife? No, uh, what you put... What you... What you...

jokes.text: Dennis says the cancer diagnosis 'is just not grabbing me right now' — delivered flatly as Charlie's mom is apparently dying.
jokes.setup: Charlie announces his mom has lung cancer, expecting sympathy.
jokes.punchline: Dennis can't muster any emotional response and admits it with clinical detachment.
jokes.explanation: Deeply character-specific to Dennis's established narcissistic sociopathy. The joke sets up the episode's Dennis arc (his inability to feel things). 'Not grabbing me right now' is a chilling and funny way to describe your friend's mom's terminal diagnosis. The character integration is what elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: That didn't sound very genuine.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No. Sorry. What was I supposed to do?

jokes.text: 'Thumbtack.' — Frank randomly blurts the word mid-conversation about scams on the elderly.
jokes.setup: The gang is in the middle of a conversation about people scamming the elderly. Frank had earlier been trying to recall a sharp word.
jokes.punchline: Frank suddenly produces 'thumbtack' — an answer to a question from minutes ago that nobody is still asking.
jokes.explanation: This is the best callback in the episode. The delayed payoff is timed impeccably — it comes in the middle of a completely unrelated conversation, which is exactly how real cognitive lapses work. Frank is validating the concern about his mind while trying to disprove it. Near-perfect economy (one word is the whole joke), perfect character integration, and the rewatch bonus is high because on a second viewing you catch the irony earlier. Approaches 8-range anchor quality.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I think the cancer thing, for whatever reason, is just not... You know, it's just not grabbing me right now.

jokes.text: Frank immediately capitulates and gives Mac's mom the hundred bucks he just said he wasn't going to give.
jokes.setup: Frank emphatically told Mac's mom he wasn't giving her money for the psychic.
jokes.punchline: Mac's mom reminds him he called her to say he changed his mind, and Frank just hands over the money without any real fight.
jokes.explanation: Functional gag demonstrating that Frank's mental slippage extends to his own decisions. Not as sharp as the 'thumbtack' joke but reinforces the theme. The 'Ah, shit. Here you go' delivery is funny in its resignation.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: My mom is dying!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Okay, calm down, calm down.

jokes.text: 'Dr. Jinx is the name of a monkey, not a man.'
jokes.setup: Charlie reveals the doctor's name is Dr. Jinx.
jokes.punchline: Mac's categorical rejection: that name belongs exclusively to a monkey, not a human physician.
jokes.explanation: Extremely quotable. The logic is absurd but delivered with total Mac-confidence. The specificity of 'a monkey, not a man' is what makes it — not 'that's a dumb name' but a precise taxonomic ruling. High economy, high quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: My mom has a doctor that can cure the cancer for 4,200 bucks, so no big deal.

jokes.text: Visual gag: Dr. Jinx practices medicine out of a residential garage surrounded by houseplants.
jokes.setup: The gang is seeking a legitimate doctor to help Charlie's mom with cancer.
jokes.punchline: The 'doctor's office' is a garage full of plants — the visual communicates everything about the legitimacy of this physician.
jokes.explanation: Strong visual setup for the Dr. Jinx sequence. The reveal that he lives/works in a garage does a lot of comedic heavy lifting before he even speaks. The houseplants pay off later when he's revealed to be a gardener.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Thumbtack.
What?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Thumbtack. We were talking about things that earlier that were sharp, and a thumbtack is sharp.

jokes.text: Dr. Jinx calls out the gang's racism about what a doctor looks like, and Mac responds: 'I normally think Asian.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Jinx points out that most people don't picture a Black man when they think of a doctor.
jokes.punchline: Instead of denying it, Mac, Dennis, and Charlie each volunteer their own specific racial assumptions, escalating into a roster of prejudices.
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny move — the characters don't deny the racism accusation, they enthusiastically confirm it with specifics. The joke is on them, not on the groups they name. The escalating list of ethnicities before 'white' is well-structured. Dr. Jinx's Cosby Show line ('Your parents ain't let you watch The Cosby Show when you was coming up?') is a great button.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Dr. Jinx is the name of a monkey, not a man.

jokes.text: 'Your parents ain't let you watch The Cosby Show when you was coming up?'
jokes.setup: Mac has just admitted he doesn't picture Black men as doctors.
jokes.punchline: Dr. Jinx diagnoses the problem as a lack of Cosby Show exposure — a culturally specific, comedically sharp retort.
jokes.explanation: Dr. Jinx's line has genuine wit — framing racism as a media-consumption problem is a sharp angle. Mac's follow-up ('My parents would never have let me watch something like that') extends the joke by implying his parents were themselves prejudiced, which is a great escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: He lives in a garage?

jokes.text: Mac: 'My parents would never have let me watch something like that.' — in response to the Cosby Show question.
jokes.setup: Dr. Jinx asks if Mac's parents let him watch The Cosby Show to explain his racial blind spots.
jokes.punchline: Mac implies his parents were themselves too racist to allow it — inadvertently revealing a worse problem than the one being diagnosed.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Mac line. He digs himself deeper without realizing it. The joke is in what's implied — that his parents' racism is the root cause, which is somehow worse. Entirely in character.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Jinx
dialogue.line: When most people think of a doctor, they don't think of a black man living in a garage surrounded by houseplants.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I normally think Asian.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah, or I think of an Indian guy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Or white.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Middle Eastern. Pretty much anything other than black.

jokes.text: Mac asks Dr. Jinx about his eczema and Dr. Jinx diagnoses it as 'sailor's rot.'
jokes.setup: Mac interrupts the visit about Charlie's mom's cancer to ask about his own skin condition.
jokes.punchline: Dr. Jinx rebrands the eczema as 'sailor's rot' — an invented, alarming medical term that implies exotic and disreputable origins.
jokes.explanation: The pivot from cancer to eczema is perfectly selfish (Mac making it about himself), and 'sailor's rot' is a brilliantly named fake condition. The name implies seafaring, disease, and moral degradation all at once.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Jinx
dialogue.line: Well, that's not eczema. What you have there, my friend, that's sailor's rot.

jokes.text: 'When was the last time you've been to Haiti?' / 'Never. I've never been to... I've been to Kensington.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Jinx tries to trace the exotic disease origin by asking about travel to Haiti.
jokes.punchline: Mac clarifies he has never left their Philadelphia neighborhood of Kensington — a notoriously grim, drug-affected area — which is somehow a satisfying answer.
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the implicit equivalence — Kensington is bad enough that it explains everything Haiti might explain. Local Philadelphia audience gets an extra layer. Mac's 'I've been to Kensington' as a confession is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Jinx
dialogue.line: When was the last time you've been to Haiti?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Never. I've never been to... I've been to Kensington.

jokes.text: Dr. Jinx asks Mac if he had 'intercourse with any hoes, ladies of the nights, or prostitutes' in Kensington. Mac says 'No... Don't worry about it. Doctor-client privilege.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Jinx is trying to establish the etiology of Mac's 'sailor's rot.'
jokes.punchline: Mac's emphatic denial collapses into 'don't worry about it' — implying the answer is yes but he won't discuss it.
jokes.explanation: The three-synonym list ('hoes, ladies of the nights, or prostitutes') is funny on its own, but Mac's rapidly collapsed denial is the real punchline. Invoking 'doctor-client privilege' to protect himself from his own inquiry is a great absurd detail.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Do you have anything from the Mother Earth that would be sprayed on me and cause me to have feelings again 'cause I'm having trouble feeling things.

jokes.text: Dennis asks Dr. Jinx if he has something from Mother Earth that would be 'sprayed on me and cause me to have feelings again.'
jokes.setup: Dr. Jinx is pitching his homeopathic remedies.
jokes.punchline: Dennis, unable to feel emotions, asks to be literally sprayed with a feeling-inducing substance — treating his sociopathy as a medical condition.
jokes.explanation: Deeply character-specific to Dennis's arc this episode and his broader characterization as a potential sociopath. The absurdist framing (a spray that installs emotions) combined with Dennis's flat, clinical delivery elevates this. It sets up the speech payoff later in the episode. High character integration because only Dennis would need this.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I think he sprayed me with Miracle-Gro.

jokes.text: Dennis asks Dr. Jinx if he has something from 'Mother Earth' that can be sprayed on him to make him 'have feelings again' because he's 'having trouble feeling things.'
jokes.setup: Mac just got treated for a physical ailment.
jokes.punchline: Dennis escalates the visit by requesting a homeopathic spray for emotional numbness — played completely straight.
jokes.explanation: Deep Dennis character work. His sociopathic inability to feel emotions — a running thread in his arc — expressed as a medical symptom he wants fixed with a topical spray is both hilarious and genuinely dark. The deadpan delivery of the request is perfect. High character integration because it only makes sense for Dennis.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Oh, she keeps a cigarette burning out on the steps outside, so she's gonna go hack a butt.

jokes.text: Gang unanimously agrees Dr. Jinx is a scam. Mac says: 'I think he sprayed me with Miracle-Gro.'
jokes.setup: The gang leaves Dr. Jinx's garage having been sprayed with an unknown substance.
jokes.punchline: Mac identifies it as a commercial plant fertilizer.
jokes.explanation: Good economy — Miracle-Gro as the great reveal. Gets a rewatch bonus because the audience knows before the characters do (via the houseplants) that this is exactly what it was. Satisfying setup payoff.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: This is a scam, okay? This is a scam. It's kneeling, standing, getting people all confused.

jokes.text: Dennis at church: 'This is ridiculous. What are we doing here?' — reacting to the religious service.
jokes.setup: Mac has brought the gang to church to pray for Charlie's mom.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's total contempt for the solution — which is played straight against Mac's earnest faith — creates the comedic tension.
jokes.explanation: Functional setup for the church sequence but not especially inventive. Dennis's skepticism here is table-setting, not a joke in itself. Competent but unremarkable.

dialogue.speaker: Psychic John
dialogue.line: I'm getting a Fa... No, I'm getting a Ba... No, I'm getting a Da... Dennis?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Dennis!

dialogue.speaker: Psychic John
dialogue.line: Is it?

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Yes, yeah, no, I'm seeing that.

jokes.text: Mrs. Kelly 'keeps a cigarette burning out on the steps outside' and 'hacks a butt' mid-mass — the lung cancer patient sneaking a smoke at church.
jokes.setup: Charlie's mom has lung cancer. They're at church to pray for her health.
jokes.punchline: She steps out of mass to smoke, and Charlie explains the Lord makes an exception for her because 'she's put her time in here.'
jokes.explanation: One of the funnier visual/behavioral gags in the episode. The irony is delicious — a lung cancer patient smoking during a prayer service for her health. Charlie's theological defense ('The Lord makes an exception for her') is a perfect absurdist button. Dark, earned, and visually funny.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Ha-- I was just out buying new shoes and I remembered I didn't want to give you that hundred bucks.

dialogue.speaker: Psychic John
dialogue.line: Yeah, and then you called me and you said you changed your mind and you'd like to give me another hundred, so where is it?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I did?

dialogue.speaker: Psychic John
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Ah, shit.

jokes.text: Mac's frantic commands during the mass — 'Now kneel,' 'stand,' 'kneel again?' — leading to Dennis's exasperated 'Son of a bitch!'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to make Dennis participate in Catholic mass rituals while Dennis resists.
jokes.punchline: The sequence of kneel-stand-kneel-stand escalates until Dennis finally explodes, then it immediately ends and Mac says 'Actually, it's over. We're standing again.'
jokes.explanation: The physical comedy of the Catholic mass's up-down ritual is used cleverly here. Dennis's 'Son of a bitch' — itself a minor blasphemy IN church — right before Mac tells him it's over is a good structural button. The 'give me money for the baskets' escalation adds another layer.

dialogue.speaker: Psychic John
dialogue.line: You have a pork chop bone in your left pocket; you have 57 cents in your right, and you clipped someone's side mirror while parking in a handicap spot.

jokes.text: Dennis complains about kneeling and standing, then is told 'it's over, we're standing again.' He says: 'Son of a bitch!'
jokes.setup: Dennis has been repeatedly forced to kneel and stand against his will throughout the service.
jokes.punchline: The moment he finally accepts kneeling, it's immediately over — he exhausted himself complying with something that was about to end.
jokes.explanation: Good running escalation on the kneeling bit with a satisfying payoff. 'Son of a bitch' as a reaction in church has an extra layer of profanity irony. Solid.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Can you conjure the dead? Can you get my dead whore wife back here so I can lay into her from the other side?

jokes.text: Mac declares the church is running a scam — 'kneeling, standing, getting people all confused' — then immediately demands Dennis give him money for the collection basket.
jokes.setup: Mac has been defending the church and demanding Dennis participate properly.
jokes.punchline: He calls the church a scam while simultaneously performing exactly the same grift — taking money from skeptical participants.
jokes.explanation: Nice self-undermining moment for Mac. He's both the enforcer of church rules and the person calling it a scam — the tension is funny and ties into the episode's scam theme. His lack of self-awareness is on brand.

dialogue.speaker: Psychic John
dialogue.line: I am feeling as if she is still living somewhere in the city with a small Mexican dog.

jokes.text: Psychic John tries to identify someone in Mac's mom's life: 'I'm getting a Fa... No, I'm getting a Ba... No, I'm getting a Da... Dennis?'
jokes.setup: Psychic John is doing a cold reading on Mac's mom.
jokes.punchline: He runs through most of the alphabet fishing for a name before landing on 'Dennis' — the most obvious cold-reading technique played completely straight.
jokes.explanation: Classic cold-reading exposure played as comedy. The fishing expedition through the alphabet is a well-known psychic con being shown in real-time. Mac's mom eating it up is what makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You're telling me that you believe that Christ comes back to life every Sunday in the form of a bowl of crackers, and then you proceed to just eat the man?

jokes.text: Psychic John says Dennis feels like 'a neighbor... or an enemy. He's a coworker, friend, he's a relative...' — covering every possible human relationship.
jokes.setup: Mac's mom is hanging on Psychic John's every word as he narrows down who Dennis is.
jokes.punchline: He lists literally every category of human relationship before she supplies the answer, exposing the con completely.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation of the cold-reading joke — after fishing for the name he now fishes for the relationship. The exhaustive list exposes the trick while Mac's mom remains oblivious. Competent.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Hey, guys, look at this. My rash is almost completely cleared up.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, my God.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Whoa.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah, look at that. Whatever he sprayed on me worked.

jokes.text: Frank buys new shoes, forgets he didn't want to give money to the psychic, calls Mac's mom to say he changed his mind and wants to give more.
jokes.setup: Frank explicitly said he wasn't giving the psychic money.
jokes.punchline: Frank forgot this entirely, went shoe shopping (suggesting his mind wandered), and voluntarily called to offer more money.
jokes.explanation: Extends the Frank mental decline thread with the added detail of the new shoes — suggesting he immediately bought more after losing the previous pairs. Character consistent and funny, though not a standout moment.

dialogue.speaker: Priest
dialogue.line: Charlie, my mother is dying of cancer and you need money to fix a statue?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: No, no, no, no, don't give me this act.

dialogue.speaker: Priest
dialogue.line: Charlie, calm down.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: No, no, no, why don't you give us some money, okay?

jokes.text: Psychic John tells Frank: 'You lost three pairs of shoes this month. You have a pork chop bone in your left pocket; you have 57 cents in your right, and you clipped someone's side mirror while parking in a handicap spot.'
jokes.setup: Frank confronts Psychic John, dismissing him as a fraud.
jokes.punchline: John rattles off a hyper-specific list of Frank's actual recent activities — all accurate, all slightly incriminating — including the pork chop bone.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Each item in the list is funny on its own (pork chop bone, 57 cents, handicap spot), and together they paint a perfect Frank portrait. The specificity is what elevates it above generic psychic jokes — this is character comedy through divination. The callback to the shoes makes it land harder. Approaches the 8.0 anchor benchmark.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: It's the Holy Trinity: beef and beer and Jesus.

jokes.text: Frank asks Psychic John to 'conjure the dead' so he can 'lay into' his dead wife 'from the other side.'
jokes.setup: John has just demonstrated impressive knowledge of Frank's life.
jokes.punchline: Frank's request isn't to speak to a deceased loved one for comfort — it's to continue an argument/grudge across the veil of death.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Frank characterization. The expected request (reconnect with a lost loved one) is completely subverted — he wants to 'lay into her from the other side.' Dark, specific, and entirely Frank. 'That dirty bitch' as his response to the possibility she's alive is a great button.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Aw, there's a dead dog in there!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Gross!

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: That's not a dog. That's my toupee, my blond toupee. I used to wear this in Miami.

jokes.text: John says he can't conjure Frank's wife because 'her spirit is still very much alive.' Frank realizes she faked her death.
jokes.setup: Frank asked the psychic to reach his dead wife; John says he can't because she's still living.
jokes.punchline: The psychic's inability to contact the dead wife is not because he's a fraud — it's because she isn't dead. This pivots the whole subplot.
jokes.explanation: Smart structural turn — the psychic being right about the wife-being-alive while wrong about everything else creates a funny inversion of expectations. The grift partially validates itself. Strong plot/comedy integration.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Padre! So good to see you. So good of you to come.

dialogue.speaker: Priest
dialogue.line: Oh... Yeah, right on, right on.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Well, it's for a good cause, isn't it? So... have some beef, have some beer. And if you feel the calling, you know, go ahead and pop that ring in the donation bucket. Although I know you won't.

jokes.text: 'She's alive... we didn't ask any questions. We never saw the body. We didn't go to the funeral.'
jokes.setup: Frank is processing the revelation that his wife may have faked her death.
jokes.punchline: The list of things they didn't do — standard funeral attendance — reveals how completely indifferent they all were to her supposed death.
jokes.explanation: The indictment of their own indifference is the joke — they didn't go to the funeral of a family member and apparently nobody thought this was odd. Dark family comedy with good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Mom, you want people to feel sorry for you, right? Then they give a lot of money. And you just don't look that sick. You gotta look sicker.

jokes.text: Dennis at church: 'Well, I'll tell you, guys. I didn't feel much in there, but I do always enjoy the little wafers.'
jokes.setup: The gang is leaving church after trying to find emotional/spiritual connection.
jokes.punchline: Dennis's only takeaway from the entire religious experience is an appreciation for communion wafers — framing the Eucharist as a snack.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dennis line — zero spiritual engagement, entirely sensory. His robotic assessment of the experience as 'didn't feel much in there' followed by a snack review is funny and sets up the transubstantiation debate perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie's Mom
dialogue.line: But I feel like it's lying.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh, it's not lying, Mrs. Kelly, because you are dying of cancer.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Yeah.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It's devouring your insides.

jokes.text: Mac: 'You're consuming the actual body of Christ.' Dennis: 'He was delicious.'
jokes.setup: Mac tries to impress upon Dennis the gravity of the Eucharist.
jokes.punchline: Dennis responds with a food review of Jesus Christ.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. Three words: 'He was delicious.' Perfect economy — it's a complete food review of the Son of God delivered with Dennis's characteristic flat affect. The structure relies on Mac providing the gravity and Dennis deflating it utterly. High quotability, high rewatch value. Comparable to 8.0 anchor jokes in economy and impact.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: It's about whether or not we're dumb enough to believe in it that matters.

jokes.text: Mac describes the Catholic belief in transubstantiation to Dennis step-by-step: 'You're eating our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ every Sunday... Christ comes back to life every Sunday in the form of a bowl of crackers...'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to defend the Eucharist after Dennis mocks it.
jokes.punchline: In the process of defending it, Mac describes the belief so literally that it sounds completely insane — the defense becomes the indictment.
jokes.explanation: 'A bowl of crackers' as the form of Christ's resurrection is the key comedic word choice. Mac's literal description destroys the mysticism he's trying to defend. Funny and irreverent without being gratuitous.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Do you feel the invisible things around you that don't really exist? Oh, it doesn't matter!

jokes.text: Mac's rash has 'almost completely cleared up' — the supposed Miracle-Gro actually worked.
jokes.setup: The gang concluded Dr. Jinx was a scam and Mac was sprayed with Miracle-Gro.
jokes.punchline: His eczema is actually improved — undercutting their certainty and potentially validating the garage doctor.
jokes.explanation: Smart callback that inverts expectations. The gang decided Dr. Jinx was definitely a fraud, but his treatment appears to be working. This keeps the show's moral ambiguity intact — nobody is fully right or wrong. The 'Oh shit' reaction from the group is the perfect response.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Dennis, that was amazing, dude. I am so proud of you. You are feeling again.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No. I meant none of it.

jokes.text: Charlie demands the priest's ring to pay for his mom's cancer treatment: 'How much is that ring worth? That looks like an expensive ring; can we have the ring?'
jokes.setup: A priest announces they need donations to repair a vandalized statue of the Virgin Mary.
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately pivots to demanding the priest's personal jewelry to fund his mother's cancer treatment.
jokes.explanation: Very Charlie — his logic is internally consistent (the ring has value, he needs money) but socially catastrophic. The aggressive shakedown of a priest is funny in its escalating specificity ('That looks like an expensive ring; can we have the ring?').

dialogue.speaker: Charlie's Mom
dialogue.line: As you know, I'm as sick as a three-legged dog on the streets of India.

jokes.text: Mac's sermon framing: 'the church's scam... is a pretty good one. It's effective... So, I say we use that model to raise money for your mom at Paddy's.'
jokes.setup: The gang has concluded both Dr. Jinx and the psychic are scams.
jokes.punchline: Mac pivots to treating organized religion as a successful business model they should replicate rather than something to be rejected.
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny gang logic — rather than rejecting the scam, they want to implement it. Mac's entrepreneurial framing of religion as a 'model' is both cynical and very specific to these characters.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie's Mom
dialogue.line: Any minute, my lungs are going to sizzle, pop, and disintegrate into a liquid lung and organ gumbo soup.

jokes.text: 'It's the Holy Trinity: beef and beer and Jesus.'
jokes.setup: Mac is pitching the beef and beer fundraiser concept.
jokes.punchline: He invokes the theological concept of the Holy Trinity to describe their fundraiser's three elements.
jokes.explanation: Very quotable. The repurposing of 'Holy Trinity' to describe a bar fundraiser is economical and funny. Mac's sincere delivery makes it land — he seems to genuinely believe this is a reasonable use of the term. High economy, high quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie's Mom
dialogue.line: Give me money. Money me. Money now. Me a money needing a lot now.

jokes.text: Frank and Dennis dig up a grave looking for money, and find: 'That's not a dog. That's my toupee, my blond toupee. I used to wear this in Miami.'
jokes.setup: Frank and Dennis are digging up what they believe is Frank's dead wife's dog's grave, expecting hidden cash.
jokes.punchline: Instead of a dog or money, they find Frank's buried blond toupee — which apparently his wife hated enough to bury.
jokes.explanation: One of the strongest jokes in the episode. The reveal is completely unexpected — a buried blond toupee from Miami, buried by his wife because she hated it. This contains multitudes: Frank's vanity, his wife's spite, the Miami backstory, and the absurdity of a toupee funeral. 'She hated this goddamn thing' as Frank's explanation is perfect. Approaches 8.0 anchor benchmark.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie's Mom
dialogue.line: We're the ones that broke the Virgin Mary statue.

jokes.text: They find cash in the grave and Frank says: 'That dirty whore.'
jokes.setup: They've discovered Frank's wife buried money with the toupee.
jokes.punchline: Frank's reaction to finding his presumably-dead wife has been hiding money is to call her a 'dirty whore' with the casual familiarity of a long marriage.
jokes.explanation: 'That dirty whore' is a recurring Frank phrase that always works. Here it's especially funny because it's his response to discovering his wife's financial duplicity from beyond the apparent grave. The character-specificity is high even if the construction is simple.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Jinx
dialogue.line: I never actually said I was a doctor.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: He is the goddamn church gardener.

jokes.text: Frank tells Dennis to get Daryl on the phone — calling Dennis 'Daryl' — 'Dennis, Dennis, goddamn it!' Frank doesn't know his own son's name in the moment.
jokes.setup: Frank's mental decline has been a running thread.
jokes.punchline: He calls his own son by the wrong name before correcting himself — another data point in the Frank-is-losing-it arc.
jokes.explanation: Consistent with Frank's established decline but not as inventive as the 'thumbtack' joke. Works as a callback and escalation but doesn't add much new.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Jinx
dialogue.line: You had my back up against the wall, I had to spray you with a heavy dose of pesticide.

jokes.text: Mr. Juarez reappears — the Mexican man whose house the gang burned down, forcing him to take their mansion — and reveals he had to move out because property taxes were too expensive.
jokes.setup: Frank recognizes Mr. Juarez from a previous incident where the gang destroyed his home.
jokes.punchline: The ostensible compensation (a mansion) became its own burden — Mr. Juarez had to leave due to property taxes — and he's now back working near his old neighborhood.
jokes.explanation: Dark callback to past gang crimes. The irony that their 'compensation' caused more problems is very Always Sunny. The quinceañera mention is a nice character detail. Gets a rewatch bonus for long-time fans.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Dennis. Dennis!

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Mom's alive. She faked her own death to steal Frank's money, and we think it's buried in her grave.

jokes.text: Frank: 'Property taxes — paying for what you already own? Now, that's a scam.'
jokes.setup: Mr. Juarez explains he had to leave the mansion because of property taxes.
jokes.punchline: Frank ties property taxes into the episode's scam theme with a pithy one-liner.
jokes.explanation: Good economy and ties the episode's scam theme together. The observation itself is not novel but Frank's confident delivery and the callback to the episode's thesis make it land. Mildly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Ah, shit! No! No! Mommy, Mommy!

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Ah! I grifted ya!

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: What are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I paid off the psychic. I buried the money in the dog grave. My mommy, my mommy's a skeleton!

jokes.text: Mac to the priest at the beef and beer: 'And if you feel the calling, you know, go ahead and pop that ring in the donation bucket. Although I know you won't. All right. Have a good time. We're both playing the same game, I-I totally get it.'
jokes.setup: Mac is running the beef and beer fundraiser modeled on the church.
jokes.punchline: He invites the priest to donate his ring, then immediately acknowledges they're both con men running parallel grifts — a moment of professional respect between scammers.
jokes.explanation: Sharp callback to Charlie's ring-demand from the church scene, now inverted — Mac is asking for the ring as a peer negotiation. 'We're both playing the same game' as the thesis statement of the episode's scam theme is well-integrated. The callback payoff on the ring is earned.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: You made me dig up my dead mother because I said you were losing it?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Score one for the old people. Ha ha!

jokes.text: Dee making up Mrs. Kelly to look sicker, applying a bald cap and fake lesions: 'I don't know why I have to wear all this makeup, and wear a bald cap.'
jokes.setup: The gang is preparing Mrs. Kelly to appear sicker for the fundraiser to maximize donations.
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Kelly objects to the elaborate sick-person disguise; Dee and Charlie explain it's 'basic Hollywood stuff.'
jokes.explanation: Good cringe setup — dressing up a genuinely sick woman to look sicker for more money is exactly the gang's brand of callous pragmatism. The visual of the bald cap and lesions is the joke.

jokes.text: Charlie's defense of the makeup scheme: 'It's not lying, Mrs. Kelly, because you are dying of cancer. Yeah. It's devouring your insides. But we need for it to devour your outside, so it plays better for our audience.'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Kelly says the disguise feels like lying.
jokes.punchline: Charlie argues it's not lying — she really is dying — they just need the visual to match the internal reality for theatrical purposes.
jokes.explanation: Very strong Charlie logic — the distinction between 'dying on the inside' and 'we need it to devour your outside' is both horrifying and hilarious. The theatrical framing ('plays better for our audience') is a great dark euphemism. High character integration because this brand of well-meaning cruelty is pure Charlie.

jokes.text: Artemis smoking weed in front of the lung cancer patient at the beef and beer: 'It's not tobacco.' / 'I realize it's not tobacco.'
jokes.setup: Dee tells Artemis she can't smoke in front of the lung cancer patient.
jokes.punchline: Artemis acknowledges it's not tobacco (implying it's marijuana) as if that addresses the concern, then Dee has to escalate to 'she's already...' to explain why it's still bad.
jokes.explanation: Artemis's total obliviousness is funny — she thinks specifying it's not tobacco resolves the concern. The 'She can recover. She can beat it' rationalization is a great Artemis button.

jokes.text: Dr. Jinx has a band named after himself performing at the beef and beer: 'We are Dr. Jinx... The man with a band named after himself.'
jokes.setup: The beef and beer fundraiser has begun.
jokes.punchline: Dr. Jinx has arrived not just as a doctor/gardener but as the frontman of a band named Dr. Jinx — the character refuses to be contained by any single grift.
jokes.explanation: The expansion of Dr. Jinx from garage physician to band frontman is a great absurdist escalation of the character. Mac's deadpan MC introduction 'The man with a band named after himself' is a funny observation that undercuts the grandiosity.

jokes.text: Dennis's 'faith' speech: 'It's not about whether something is true, or based in fact, or reality, or the laws of physics, or nature, or even basic common sense. It's about whether or not we're dumb enough to believe in it that matters.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is giving a fundraiser speech that's supposed to inspire charitable giving for Charlie's mom.
jokes.punchline: Instead of a sincere faith message, Dennis describes belief as a form of stupidity — and seems to find this liberating.
jokes.explanation: Dennis's speech is a great comedic piece — it starts sounding like it might be sincere, then slides into 'whether or not we're dumb enough to believe in it.' The list 'laws of physics, or nature, or even basic common sense' escalates perfectly. This is Dennis finding emotion through cynicism, which is a perfect character beat. High structure, high character integration.

jokes.text: Dennis's escalating revival-preacher performance: 'Ladies and gentlemen, if we believe... if we just believe... then we can do anything!' — delivered with manic energy.
jokes.setup: Dennis's detached, cynical speech is turning into something unintentionally passionate.
jokes.punchline: He builds to a full evangelical-style crescendo, apparently accessing emotion despite himself — or performing emotion so hard he's lost track of whether it's real.
jokes.explanation: The payoff on Dennis's emotional arc is well-earned. He asked Dr. Jinx for a feeling-spray and now he's accidentally feeling things through a cynical scam speech. The escalation from deadpan to evangelical frenzy is a great performance joke. Ties together multiple threads.

jokes.text: 'Do you feel the invisible things around you that don't really exist? Oh, it doesn't matter!'
jokes.setup: Dennis's speech has reached peak evangelical energy.
jokes.punchline: He invites the crowd to feel 'invisible things that don't really exist' and then immediately dismisses the question of their existence as irrelevant.
jokes.explanation: The 'invisible things around you that don't really exist' followed by 'Oh, it doesn't matter!' is the thematic core of the episode delivered as comedy. Dennis is simultaneously mocking and embodying faith. The concession 'it doesn't matter' is both nihilistic and strangely moving, which is what makes it funny.

jokes.text: Post-speech, Charlie: 'I am so proud of you. You are feeling again.' Dennis: 'No. I meant none of it.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is moved by Dennis's apparent emotional breakthrough.
jokes.punchline: Dennis flatly denies any genuine feeling — 'I meant none of it' — undercutting the entire arc.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Dennis button. After a whole episode arc about emotional numbness, after what appeared to be a breakthrough, four words: 'No. I meant none of it.' This is Dennis Reynolds in complete form — the horror and comedy of his sociopathy encapsulated. The economy is exceptional, the character integration is as high as it gets. Among the best lines in the episode. Approaches the top anchor benchmark.

jokes.text: Mrs. Kelly reads the speech: 'I'm as sick as a three-legged dog on the streets of India.'
jokes.setup: The gang wrote Mrs. Kelly a speech for the fundraiser to maximize sympathy donations.
jokes.punchline: The speech's first line is a grotesquely specific, oddly exotic simile for her illness.
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'three-legged dog on the streets of India' is what makes it. It's so specific and so unnecessary — why India? — that it reveals the gang's tin ear for genuine sympathy. Quotable, absurdist, and character-revealing.

jokes.text: Second line of the speech: 'Any minute, my lungs are going to sizzle, pop, and disintegrate into a liquid lung and organ gumbo soup.'
jokes.setup: The gang's sympathy speech continues.
jokes.punchline: 'Liquid lung and organ gumbo soup' — a grotesque food metaphor for organ failure that reveals the speech was clearly written by someone (Charlie) with no emotional intelligence.
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode. 'Liquid lung and organ gumbo soup' is specifically horrible — combining medical horror with Cajun cuisine. It's immediately clear this was written by Charlie (the gumbo language, the specificity of 'sizzle, pop'). High originality because nobody else would phrase lung failure this way. Very quotable.

jokes.text: Dee, aside: 'That was my line.'
jokes.setup: Mrs. Kelly has just read the horrific 'liquid lung and organ gumbo soup' line.
jokes.punchline: Dee claims credit for it — implying that the most grotesque line in the speech is hers, not Charlie's.
jokes.explanation: Perfect button. 'That was my line' inverts our expectation (Charlie seemed most likely to write this) and reveals Dee's pride in the grotesque work. The economy is near-perfect — three words do everything. Rewatch bonus because on second viewing you're listening for whose authorship is implied.

jokes.text: The money line of the speech: 'Give me money. Money me. Money now. Me a money needing a lot now.' — then Charlie admits: 'That was Charlie's line.'
jokes.setup: After the elaborate sympathy speech, they get to the actual ask.
jokes.punchline: The money ask devolves into Yoda-speak caveman syntax: 'Money me. Money now. Me a money needing a lot now.' Charlie's literary fingerprints are all over it.
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode, possibly the best. 'Money me. Money now. Me a money needing a lot now.' is completely specific to Charlie's established near-illiteracy and chaotic syntax. The escalating syntactic breakdown is perfectly constructed — it gets worse with each iteration. The self-citation ('That was Charlie's line') is a perfect self-aware button. This is a legitimately great sitcom joke. Very high character integration — only Charlie's writing could look like this.

jokes.text: Mrs. Kelly confesses to the congregation that she doesn't have cancer — and that they're the ones who broke the Virgin Mary statue.
jokes.setup: The whole episode has been built around Mrs. Kelly's cancer diagnosis driving everyone's actions.
jokes.punchline: She doesn't have cancer — the whole premise was a manipulation, and furthermore she and Mac's mom broke the statue they'd been asked to donate to.
jokes.explanation: Strong structural payoff — the cancer reveal recontextualizes the whole episode and ties together the statue subplot. The double twist (no cancer + they broke the statue) is well-structured. The moms out-grifted the gang.

jokes.text: Mac: 'You could've just told me the story about hitting the statue. I mean, where did you come up with this idea?' Mrs. Kelly: 'Well, I learned everything by watching you.'
jokes.setup: Mac is indignant that his mom invented a cancer lie instead of just asking for help.
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Kelly reveals she learned the manipulation playbook from watching Mac himself — the gang corrupted their own parents.
jokes.explanation: Great thematic button on the episode's scam theme. 'I learned everything by watching you' is the perfect karmic inversion — the gang raised their parents to grift. Mac's moral indignation is completely undermined. Strong structure and high character integration.

jokes.text: 'Well, I learned everything by watching you.' — Mrs. Mac to the priest, after he calls her scam 'crazy.'
jokes.setup: The priest says the scheme to fake cancer to raise money was crazy.
jokes.punchline: Mrs. Mac turns it on the priest: she learned it from watching him — the church's own fundraising model inspired the scam.
jokes.explanation: A satisfying thematic callback. 'I learned everything by watching you' is a classic after-school-special inversion — usually said by a child to a drug-using parent. Here it's said to a priest about grifting techniques. The structure is clean and the economy is good.

jokes.text: It's revealed that 'Dr. Jinx' is actually the church gardener — he explicitly said he was never a doctor.
jokes.setup: Dr. Jinx has been treating patients throughout the episode.
jokes.punchline: He's the church gardener. His 'practice' was gardening-based. The gang went to a gardener for cancer treatment.
jokes.explanation: Excellent payoff on the Dr. Jinx setup. The clues were all there (garage, houseplants, Miracle-Gro spray) but the gardener reveal lands as a genuine surprise. 'I never actually said I was a doctor' is the perfect technical defense. The pesticide reveal (not Miracle-Gro but actual pesticide) is a great escalation that retroactively worsens what happened to Mac.

jokes.text: Dr. Jinx reveals he sprayed Mac with pesticide, not Miracle-Gro: 'I had to spray you with a heavy dose of pesticide. Put some aloe vera gel on there, a little bit of vitamin D...'
jokes.setup: Mac's rash cleared up and everyone briefly accepted Dr. Jinx might be legitimate.
jokes.punchline: He sprayed Mac with pesticide. The rash clearing was likely because a skin condition was replaced by a chemical burn, and he's now casually prescribing aloe.
jokes.explanation: Great escalation of the Miracle-Gro joke — it wasn't plant food, it was pesticide. The implication that Mac may have been poisoned, combined with Dr. Jinx's casual follow-up prescription of aloe and vitamin D, is very funny. 'Mother Earth don't play' resonates as a callback.

jokes.text: Dr. Jinx then starts diagnosing Charlie again mid-confession: 'Put some aloe vera gel on there, a little bit of vitamin D—'
jokes.setup: Dr. Jinx has just admitted he's not a doctor.
jokes.punchline: He immediately slides back into offering medical advice — still can't stop himself from playing the role.
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat that shows Dr. Jinx can't help himself — the role of doctor has become instinct. 'Don't get a diagnosis from him now' is a good reaction line from Mac.

jokes.text: Frank opens what he believes is Frank's wife's grave, expecting money. Instead: 'No! No! Mommy, Mommy! Ah! I grifted ya!'
jokes.setup: The gang has been told Frank's wife is alive and her money is buried in her grave. They're about to open the coffin.
jokes.punchline: The body IS in there — Frank's wife's actual skeleton. It was a double-cross by Frank's wife, who is very much alive and watching.
jokes.explanation: Strong visual/structural punchline. The skeleton in the coffin is a great reversal — the whole sequence has been building toward money, and the punchline is a corpse. Frank's traumatic 'Mommy, Mommy!' is funny in its vulnerability. The appearance of the living wife ('I grifted ya!') is a perfect button.

jokes.text: Frank: 'This is such a perfect place for that bitch to hide my money.'
jokes.setup: The gang is now at a graveyard, about to dig up Barbara's (Frank's supposedly dead wife's) coffin looking for hidden money.
jokes.punchline: Frank's characterization of his dead wife's grave as 'a perfect place for that bitch to hide my money' treats a cemetery as a financial dispute location.
jokes.explanation: Frank graverobbing his own wife's grave and describing it as a 'perfect hiding spot' is very on-brand. The affectionate hostility — 'that bitch' — combined with the genuine admiration for her strategy is a great character note.

jokes.text: Frank's wife reveals the whole thing was a long con: she paid off the psychic, buried decoy money in the dog grave — all to mess with Frank because he said she was 'slipping.'
jokes.setup: The whole subplot has been Frank convinced his dead wife is actually alive and hiding money.
jokes.punchline: She is alive, but everything they 'found' was planted — the entire hunt was engineered to humiliate Frank and prove she's not losing her mind.
jokes.explanation: Elegant full-episode payoff. The long con reveals that everything we watched was engineered — the psychic, the dog grave money, all of it. 'I grifted your asses good because you said I was slipping' is a perfect 'Score one for the old people' moment. The structural cleverness of using the episode's own scam theme against the gang is well-executed.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Show me the money, show me the money...' — chanting as Charlie opens the coffin.
jokes.setup: Charlie is about to crack open the coffin.
jokes.punchline: Mac is chanting 'Show me the money' like a sports fan — an absurd pop culture invocation at a grave opening.
jokes.explanation: Functional energy gag. The 'Show me the money' chant at a coffin opening is a decent absurd detail but doesn't rise above functional. The energy of the scene carries it.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'I feel too much!' — after opening a coffin and seeing his mother's skeleton.
jokes.setup: Throughout the episode, Dennis has been unable to feel emotions. He asked Dr. Jinx for an emotion-spray.
jokes.punchline: The sight of his mother's skeleton is what finally breaks through his emotional numbness — the most traumatic possible stimulus unlocks his feelings.
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode and one of the strongest jokes in the series' formula. Dennis spent the entire episode unable to feel anything — not his friend's mom's cancer diagnosis, not a church service, not what appeared to be a genuine emotional speech. The thing that finally cracks him open is seeing his mother's skeleton. 'I feel too much!' is the inversion of everything the episode built toward. Perfect structure — the whole episode is the setup. Perfect economy — three words do the work of a full arc. Perfect character integration — this is the most Dennis Reynolds resolution possible. This is what earning a 9 looks like.

jokes.text: Frank's wife: 'Score one for the old people.'
jokes.setup: The gang has been outsmarted by an elderly woman who faked her death and ran a months-long con.
jokes.punchline: Her victory declaration is 'score one for the old people' — the most understated possible celebration of an extraordinary grift.
jokes.explanation: Good button on the whole subplot. The understatement of 'score one for the old people' after an elaborate multi-month deception is funny in its modesty. Ties into the episode's theme of old people being underestimated.

jokes.text: Final line — Frank, standing at a grave having just been shown his dead wife: 'Wait a minute. What the hell happened to my shoes?'
jokes.setup: The episode ends with Frank having just experienced an enormous emotional and logistical shock.
jokes.punchline: His mind immediately snaps back to the shoes — not the living wife, not the grave, not the grift. The shoes.
jokes.explanation: Exceptional episode closer. After everything — the grave, the wife's return, the revelation that he was grifted — Frank's first concern is his missing shoes. This is both the perfect Frank callback and a beautiful comedic compression of his character: the trivial overwhelms the profound for him. The structure is essentially the whole episode compressed into one line. Among the best closing jokes the show does.

tmdb_overview: Mac, Charlie and Dee struggle with their faith as Charlie's mom fights cancer. Meanwhile, Frank loses his memory amidst a search for buried treasure.
